passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying doses of a novel cognitive enhancer on reaction time in healthy adults. A double‑blind, randomized controlled trial enrolled 120 participants, who were assigned to one of four groups: a placebo control, a low‑dose (10 mg), a medium‑dose (20 mg), or a high‑dose (40 mg) treatment. Each participant completed a computerized Stroop task before and after a single dose. Mean reaction times (ms) and standard deviations (SD) were recorded. The control group had a mean post‑dose reaction time of 650 ms (SD 45). The low‑dose group improved to 620 ms (SD 50), the medium‑dose group to 590 ms (SD 55), and the high‑dose group to 560 ms (SD 60). The researchers noted a dose‑dependent trend, with the high‑dose group showing the greatest reduction in reaction time. However, the high‑dose group also exhibited the largest variability. The authors suggested that while the enhancer improves cognitive speed, higher doses may introduce inconsistent effects, warranting further investigation into optimal dosing and safety.
stem: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time after receiving the dose?
explanation: The high‑dose group (40 mg) had the lowest mean reaction time of 560 ms, indicating the greatest improvement.
trap: Picking the control group because 650 ms is the largest number, forgetting that a lower reaction time means faster performance.

stem: Which variable is the independent variable in this study?
explanation: Correct: B) The researchers manipulated the dose (placebo, 10, 20, 40 mg) and observed its effect on reaction time. Why the others are wrong: A) Reaction time is the measured outcome (dependent variable). C) Baseline reaction time is a pre-dose measurement, not something the researchers assigned. D) The standard deviation is a summary statistic of the results, not a manipulated factor.
trap: Picking reaction time because it is the headline measurement; it is the outcome that responds to the manipulated dose, not the independent variable.

trap: Dividing the 90 ms difference by the high-dose value (560 ms) gives about 16% and tempts rounding to 15%; the reference for the reduction is the control value of 650 ms.

stem: Which statement is supported by the table?

options.A: Mean reaction time was 30 ms lower with each successively higher dose group.
options.B: The high-dose group had a smaller SD than the control group.
options.C: The low-dose group had the highest mean reaction time of the four groups.
options.D: The medium-dose group had the lowest SD.

explanation: Correct: A) The means are 650, 620, 590, 560 ms, a 30 ms drop at each step. Why the others are wrong: B) High-dose SD is 60 ms, larger than the control's 45 ms. C) The control group (650 ms) had the highest mean; low dose was 620 ms. D) The control group had the lowest SD (45 ms); medium dose was 55 ms.
trap: Assuming the largest improvement also came with the most consistent performance, when SD actually rose with dose.
